text.p: These are the key facts about Madagascar, where state radio said on Sunday more than 100 people were killed by a cyclone that swept through the southern tip of the island.
Officials said many thousands of people were homeless after their rural dwellings were flattened by Cyclone Gretelle which struck the area on Friday night.
POPULATION: Estimated at 12,092,000 in mid-1993. Annual growth rate of 3.1 percent.
LANGUAGES: Malagasy, closed related to Malay, and French.
AREA: 587,041 square km (226,658 square miles). Madagascar is an island in the Indian Ocean about 400 km (250 miles) off the coast of Mozambique.
CAPITAL: Antananarivo, population estimated at 662,585 in 1985.
ARMED FORCES: In 1993 the total number of men in the armed forces were estimated at 21,000. There is a paramilitary gendarmerie of 7,500 men.

RELIGION: It is estimated that more than 50 percent of the population follow traditional animist beliefs. Some 43 percent are Christians -- about half of whom are Roman Catholics -- and the remainder are Moslems.
ECONOMY: The economy is based on cultivation of paddy rice, coffee, vanilla and cloves for export.

Population growth outstripped economic growth for most years since the late 1970s. The World Bank classified Madagascar as one of the world's 13 poorest countries in 1992 -- in that year gross national product, measured at 1990-1992 prices, was $2.8 billion or $230 per head.

HISTORY: Madagascar's people arrived in several waves of settlement from Africa and Indonesia, beginning about 1,500 years ago. France annexed Madagascar in 1896 after six years of war against the independent monarchy. Up to 80,000 people were killed in anti-French riots in 1947 and Madagascar finally won independence in 1960 under the pro-French regime of Philbert Tsiranana.

Tsiranana resigned as president in 1972 and handed over power to the armed forces. After political turmoil during three years of military rule, navy commander Didier Ratsiraka, a left-wing nationalist, became head of the military junta in 1975. A referendum confirmed him as president for a seven-year term. He was re-elected in 1982 and in 1989.

The 1989 elections were contested by opposition candidates and protests erupted against Ratsiraka in 1990 and 1991, demanding his resignation. Up to 130 died when security forces fired on protestors marching on the Presidential palace on August 10, 1991 to demand Ratsiraka's resignation. A settlement which relinquished all Ratsiraka's executive powers was reached on October 31, 1991.
A referendum for a new constitution was approved in August 1992, paving the way for presidential polls. Albert Zafy won the presidential elections in the second round in February 1993.
The national assembly impeached Zafy last July for contravening the constitution and exceeding his powers.
Ratsiraka returned to Madagascar late last year from 20 months' voluntary exile in France to contest the subsequent election, which led to a December 29 run-off between the two former presidents.

The announcement of results was suspended -- after most of them had been broadcast -- when Zafy complained that the figures were being manipulated in favour Ratsiraka. Officials said the announcement of the final result was expected by the end of January or early February.
